name: Shackleton rim (Peak Near Shackleton)
why: The emblematic polar site: the rim sees the Sun most of the year while the crater floor never does. The ideal test of light versus ice.
coord_source: IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature (crater centre)
notes: Artemis III candidate region in the 2022 list (not in the 2024 list of nine). Exact landing point not published; feature centre used.

name: IM-2 Athena
why: Highest-latitude landing ever. The closest real test of what this tool simulates.
notes: Landed March 2025 and came to rest on its side in a crater.

name: Statio Shiv Shakti (Chandrayaan-3)
why: First landing near the south pole (August 2023). Shows that sites near 70 S are reachable.

name: IM-1 Odysseus
why: First commercial landing and first US landing since 1972, already at 80 S, with real failure data.
notes: Landed February 2024. About 0.13 deg from the 80 S edge of the 20 m map, so part of its window is filled from coarser data.

name: Apollo 17, Taurus-Littrow
why: Last and longest crewed landing. A valley between massifs, good for testing real horizons.

name: Apollo 11, Mare Tranquillitatis
why: The first human landing, recognised by every judge. The validation anchor.

name: Blue Ghost M1, Mare Crisium
why: First fully successful commercial mission, through a complete lunar day.

name: Apollo 15, Hadley Rille
why: Dramatic relief (Apennine mountains and a rille). First use of the Lunar Roving Vehicle.

name: SLIM (Shioli)
why: Precision landing about 55 m from target: proof that choosing the point matters.

name: Chang'e 6, Apollo basin (Statio Tianjiang)
why: First sample return from the far side.

name: Chang'e 4, Von Karman (Statio Tianhe)
why: First far-side landing. No line of sight to Earth, so a good case for the Earth requirement.

name: Apollo 16, Descartes
why: The only highland landing.

name: Apollo 12, Oceanus Procellarum
why: Precision landing on a mare, next to an older probe (Surveyor 3).

name: Chang'e 3, Mare Imbrium
why: First soft landing in 37 years, at mid-northern latitude.

name: Apollo 14, Fra Mauro
why: Imbrium basin ejecta terrain, rolling relief.

name: de Gerlache Rim 2
why: Artemis III candidate region almost at the pole, with narrow rims and long shadows.

name: Slater Plain
why: Flat candidate terrain, a contrast to the rim sites.

name: Haworth
why: Large crater with permanent shadow and lit rims.
notes: To be confirmed: the Gazetteer centre looks inconsistent with the crater diameter.

name: Mons Malapert (Malapert Massif)
why: A mountain with direct line of sight to Earth, good for communication.

name: Mons Mouton (plateau)
why: The region where IM-2 landed: links past and future.
